Subject: Deployment traffic ownership and failure-mode clarifications

Hi Ben,

Thanks for the RFI packet you sent earlier. As part of Sanctuary Health's procurement review we have a few follow-ups specifically focused on traffic ownership and failure-mode behavior for the Private deployment option (VPC + sidecar). Our security architects asked for concise answers to the items below so we can model network boundaries for our architecture review and risk register: 

1) Ownership model: which components in Redwood's Private deployment initiate outbound connections to external services (metrics, control-plane telemetry, image registries)? Are these under customer-managed NAT/egress or do you originate from Redwood-managed endpoints?

2) Sidecar egress behavior: does the sidecar pod/proxy ever open sockets to external networks on behalf of hosted models (e.g., for telemetry, model fetch, plugin calls)? If so, can you list domains/IP ranges and whether connections are reestablished on failover?

3) Cross-zone failover: when a workload fails over between AZs/zones, what is the time-to-reconnect for TCP streams and how are in-flight KV/cache entries reconciled? Any expected transient egress during failover?

4) Evidence: can you provide a network diagram that highlights customer-controlled vs Redwood-controlled egress, a sample egress allowlist CSV, and a short threat-model summary that maps high-level attacker objectives to controls in the deployment topology?

We need this material for our SOC/scoping call next Thursday (4/5). If you can send a written response and the artifacts by EOD Monday (4/1) that would be ideal.

Thanks,
Aditi Rao
Lead Security Engineer
Sanctuary Health

Appreciate the clear ask. I've looped in Mina (infra/security) and Karthik (product) to make sure we give you precise, evidence-backed answers. High level summary below; full attachments in the follow-up.

Quick answers (short):
- Ownership: Customer-managed egress. All data-plane outbound traffic from model inference workers originates from customer VPC subnets; control-plane telemetry uses an optional, customer-configurable egress path (default: customer NAT).
- Sidecar: Our sidecar only opens outbound connections to image registries and to a small set of telemetry/control endpoints we publish — it will never proxy arbitrary external traffic.
- Failover: TCP reconnection time is typically <8s for cold failover across AZs; KV reconciliation is eventual (seconds) with oplog replay. We include guardrails to avoid splat egress.

I'll send the diagram + allowlist + short threat-model summary in my next mail (attachments: redwood-deployment-traffic-overview-v1.pdf, sanctuary-egress-rules.csv, deployment-topology-3zone.svg). If those look good, let's put a 30-min scoping slot on Thursday.

Ben / Karthik —

I reviewed the attachments and suggested tightened language below for the customer deliverable. I'm pasting the version I recommend we send to Sanctuary; it's phrased to be compatible with their procurement/SOC reviewers and includes conservative numbers. Feel free to paste into your reply.

Suggested response (technical):

1) Ownership model
- Data plane (inference workers & KV caches): All outbound connections that originate from inference worker processes and their sidecars are sourced from the customer's private subnets and egress via customer-managed NAT/GW by default. Redwood's Private deployment installs a lightweight sidecar that is configured by default to use the node's networking namespace; it does not create an independent public egress path. Customers can opt to route telemetry to a Redwood-managed endpoint for convenience; this is explicitly configurable and disabled by default.

2) Sidecar egress behavior
- The sidecar only initiates outbound connections for: model artifact fetches (from configured registries), image pulls, and optional telemetry (push) to configured endpoints. Sidecar outbound destinations are limited to a curated allowlist; we publish domains and IP ranges as part of the onboarding packet (sample attached). The sidecar will not proxy arbitrary customer traffic or serve as a general-purpose forward proxy.

3) Cross-zone failover and transient egress
- Failover model: a primary inference pod failing triggers scheduler-driven restart and traffic shift to warm standby(s). Observed median connection reestablishment for client TCP sessions (reconnect + session rehydrate) is 2–6 seconds; under worst-case cold restart we account for up to 12s before full KV sync completes. KV/cached state reconciliation uses an write-ahead log (oplog) with idempotent replay; transient duplicates are possible and our at-most-once semantics are enforced at the service layer where required.
- Transient egress: during failover, short-lived control-plane heartbeats and artifact fetch retries may generate ephemeral external connections (seconds). These are constrained to the allowlist and are limited in rate.

4) Threat-model mapping (high level)
- Attacker objective: exfiltrate inference input/outputs via egress path
  Controls: customer-managed NAT, allowlists, sidecar process isolation, TLS everywhere, mTLS to control-plane where applicable, and per-token telemetry filtering.
- Attacker objective: supply-chain compromise via model registry
  Controls: signed artifacts, registry allowlist, reproducible artifact hashes and verification at load time.

Artifacts we will provide: deployment-topology-3zone.svg (annotated), redwood-deployment-traffic-overview-v1.pdf (narrative), sanctuary-egress-rules.csv (sample allowlist), and an index of evidence for auditors (audit-evidence-index.txt).

If you want tighter SLA numbers for reconnection (e.g., hard SLOs), we can extract traces from the dedicated cluster used in your PoC and include p50/p95 reconnection curves.

Mina
Senior Infrastructure Security Engineer
Redwood Inference

Hi Aditi —

Thanks for the scoped questions. Please find answers below (copied from our infra team) and the requested artifacts attached. We aimed to keep the language procurement-friendly while preserving technical accuracy.

1) Ownership model
- Data-plane egress: outbound traffic from inference workers and KV caches originates from customer VPC subnets and uses customer-managed NAT by default. Our sidecar operates in the node/network namespace and does not create a separate public egress path unless explicitly configured by the customer (opt-in). Redwood-managed control-plane endpoints are optional and used only where customers enable them; we can provide a private peering option for control-plane telemetry if needed.

2) Sidecar egress behavior
- Sidecar outbound activity is limited to: model artifact fetches (from allowed registries), container image pulls, and optional telemetry/control-plane pushes. We publish a curated allowlist (sample attached) and redact sensitive telemetry fields by default. The sidecar is not a generic proxy and will not forward arbitrary customer traffic.

3) Cross-zone failover & KV reconciliation
- Observed reconnection behavior: median reconnect + session rehydrate 2–6s; worst-case cold restart accounted as up to 12s before KV reconciliation finalizes. KV reconciliation uses WAL/oplog replay with idempotent application; our platform applies rate-limiting and backoff to control artifact fetch retries during recovery to prevent large-scale simultaneous external connections.

4) Threat-model summary (high level)
- Exfiltration via egress: mitigated by customer-controlled egress, allowlists, TLS/mTLS, sidecar isolation, and telemetry filtering.
- Supply-chain risks: mitigated by signed artifacts, registries in an allowlist, and artifact verification during load.

Attachments included: redwood-deployment-traffic-overview-v1.pdf (narrative), deployment-topology-3zone.svg (annotated diagram), sanctuary-egress-rules.csv (sample allowlist), audit-evidence-index.txt (evidence index). We can also produce a short p50/p95 reconnection graph from a PoC cluster if your SOC team wants SLA-bound numbers.
